content:
Multiple Dropbox users received emails from the cloud storage company notifying them that their accounts had been accessed by an unauthorised party due to a security vulnerability.

The root cause appears to be that Dropbox lacked an identity verification process when an attacker set up a single sign-on option through a third-party company...

Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on social media platform X.

Other Dropbox users also reported receiving the same email, in which the company stated that the incident was caused by an issue with the single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo ID.

However, while Dropbox has pointed the finger at the vulnerability in Lenovo's email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be Dropbox itself failing to require users to verify new SSOs using their existing sign-in method, as reported by The CyberSec Guru.

  • Reconnaissance/target selection: The attacker collects target email addresses (via leaked databases, LinkedIn, customer lists, etc.—email addresses are essentially public information).
  • Malicious IdP registration: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID with victim@example.com. Because Lenovo's verification steps are missing or can be bypassed, access to the victim's mailbox is not required. The display name is set to a disposable name—one victim who successfully recovered their impersonated account discovered the name was that of the late NFL broadcaster "John Madden"; names of this kind are clearly characteristic of large-scale, low-cost registrations.
  • Federated login: The attacker clicks "Continue with Lenovo" on Dropbox. Lenovo's authorisation server issues a token, in which the email claim matches the victim's Dropbox account.
  • Implicit account linking: Dropbox matches the existing account based on the email claim and issues a login session. No password was required, no additional verification step was taken, and there was no authorisation prompt asking "Link this new identity?" As far as Dropbox is concerned, a trusted IdP has already vouched for that email address.

9to5Mac's take

Although Lenovo does indeed have shortcomings in verifying email addresses, no damage would have occurred had Dropbox simply verified identities when linking them. Failing to take this step is a serious oversight.

The company has since patched the vulnerability and invalidated all sessions previously "authenticated" via Lenovo ID.
